newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PNG announces new peace plan for Bougainville.
newsitem.headline: PNG announces new peace plan for Bougainville.

text.p: Papua New Guinea has announced a new peace plan for Bougainville island and diplomatic pressure is mounting for it to stop using mercenaries to train troops to strike at secessionist rebels.
"The peace strategy assumes that a military solution to the conflict is not possible," said Minister for Provincial and Local Government Affairs Peter Barter.
"Government also recognises that peace cannot be imposed," Barter said in a statement received here on Friday.

Barter, who has been tasked with finding a peaceful solution to the nine-year conflict on Bougainville, said Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Julius Chan had endorsed the new "Peace Strategy", which should be in place by next week.
Australian and New Zealand defence ministers on Friday called on Papua New Guinea to stop using mercenaries.
"We see it as absolutely unacceptable there should be contracted mercenary forces in the South Pacific," New Zealand Defence Minister Paul East told a news conference in Canberra.
Australian Defence Minister Ian McLachlan said Australia would consider using all options to encourage Chan to reconsider the plan.

"We're not as yet making any judgments about the defence co-operation programme, but we'll be looking at all the avenues, financial and other, to make sure that we try to bring about an end to this very undesirable innovation of Sir Julius," he said.
South African mercenary firm Executive Outcomes said on Tuesday it had been sub-contracted by British consultancy Sandline International which had a contract with Papua New Guinea.

Chan said on Tuesday 40 mercenaries are currently training a small group of soldiers with the aim of launching an attack on Bougainville island, 800 km (500 miles) northeast of the Papua New Guinea capital Port Moresby.
Chan has said the mercenaries would go to Bougainville only as military advisers and would not be used in any fighting.
But East said the New Zealand government believed the mercenaries would be used for more than basic training.
"From the information we have, these mercenaries are going to be used in a manner in which we wouldn't countenance the use of Australian and New Zealand forces," East said.
Barter said the new peace plan would not be made public until Bougainvilleans and rebels have been notified.

"The peace strategy addresses the war weariness amongst most Bougainvilleans...The high levels of violent conflict within and between Bougainvillean groups must also be reduced," Barter said in a statement from Port Moresby.

Hundreds of people have been killed during the Bougainville conflict in fighting and from a lack of medical treatment. Amnesty International has reported human rights abuses by government troops and rebels.
Barter said the plan saw the restoration of "traditional authority" on Bougainville through a council of elders.
"It is paramount that the traditional leadership be restored so that the chiefs can provide the security necessary for services to be delivered to the people...," Barter said.

"Whilst the security forces will remain, as peace is gradually restored, a gradual transit will take place so that the 'law and order' responsibility is returned to the police and the traditional system of maintaining law within the society."
"Once the peace strategy is in place I do not imagine it will miraculously bring about peace overnight. It may take many years for peace and normalcy to be restored, but at least we now have a plan."
